Lessons Learned • Experimental Design: The blending of two electroactive materials requires careful experimental planning to ensure that we can test the properties of each 26 DE-EE0009099 material individually. We believe that our composite materials may have binodal electrocaloric performance (the materials may exhibit cooling at multiple temperatures) because the LCs will cool at higher temperature than the PVDF terpolymer matrix. Such a material might have unique applications. We would still like to explore this. • Corporate engagement: Our collaboration with RTRC faltered after the first year. Their effort required too many resources given the overall project size. We should have kept the work largely in-house and worked with RTRC as a consulting partner for setting up our own equipment. At the time we did not have the confidence of being able to set up our own test rig. However, we found that we could build our own test system and even integrated a thermal camera into the system. 7. Conclusions We have demonstrated the use of electrospray processing to make thin film electrocaloric devices with an electroactive PVDF terpolymer. Unlike casting, electrospray processing enables the exquisite control of thickness in morphology in ways that benefit electrocaloric performance. These thin films exhibit remarkable dielectric breakdown strength which is critical for activating the material as a solid-state cooling device. We were particularly excited to see that thin film produced by electrospray processing exhibited better electrocaloric performance than films produced by casting. We attributed this to a certain level of order imposed by the electrosprayed film. We unfortunately did not see remarkable improvements in electrocaloric performance of our films with the incorporation of LCs. We attributed this to the higher activation temperature of the LCs that we used. We believe there are opportunities to explore other LCs or these LC containing films at higher temperatures. In all, we believe that this work has advanced the processing of electrocaloric materials which is, potentially a field that is underserved by this community. With most of the research focused on identifying new materials with exceptional electroactive properties, few seemed to be addressing manufacturing of the materials into functional systems. I hope that our work will spur some of this interest in electrocaloric material manufacturing. We also note that that the PI has launched a company (membraneX) commercializing electrospray technology for manufacturing thin films. While membrane applications are the likely first beachhead market for the company, the company is agnostic to the final application of electrospray. We would welcome an opportunity to consider commercialization of this technology through membraneX, though we would need an HVAC 27 DE-EE0009099 partner. We have engaged with Trane on other discussions (after the conclusion of this project), and they might be a future partner. 8.
